BPC-157 is the deliberately harder half of this pair. There is no approved product, no human trial in anything held here, and three sources that describe three different regimens. The architecture's job on this record is to keep all of that visible at once without letting volume of discussion read as weight of evidence. Updated 14 September 2026: the interstitial cystitis study (SRC-030) is now held in full and read; the intravenous pilot (SRC-029) is held only as an owner transcription whose body is unverified, so it stays at abstract level; the file supplied for the knee-pain study (SRC-031) was a different article, so that study also stays at abstract level. Three primary preclinical studies mapped by the orthopaedic systematic review (SRC-032) were read in full under CC BY and are cited directly (BPC-012 to BPC-014); the review itself is cited only for the shape of the literature (BPC-011); four ClinicalTrials.gov registrations are recorded as trials with no results; what could not be read is recorded as gaps.

compound.shortDescription: A synthetic fifteen-amino-acid peptide, described by the sources held here as derived from a protein found in human gastric juice. Very widely discussed, almost entirely on animal research: a literature screen identified three small uncontrolled human studies and no approved product anywhere.
compound.simpleSummary:
BPC-157 is a short synthetic peptide. The sources held here describe it as a fragment of a larger protein found in stomach fluid, which is where the name comes from: body protection compound.

It is discussed more than almost any other compound in this field, largely in the context of healing — tendons, ligaments, muscle, gut lining, skin. There is a considerable body of laboratory and animal work behind those claims, and the practitioner sources held here are careful about how they say it: one describes the effects as observed "in laboratory studies".

**Research in people is very limited.** A search of the PubMed medical literature database on 13 September 2026 returned 230 records mentioning the compound. Reading through them, three were studies in people: two people given it intravenously, twelve women given it for a bladder condition, and a review of the records of seventeen patients given it in the knee. Thirty-one people in total, across three studies, none of which had a comparison group. That last point matters more than the numbers. Without a comparison group, a study cannot tell whether the people who got better did so because of the treatment.

Almost everything else is animal research. As of 15 September 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists three placebo- or sham-controlled studies of BPC-157 in people — one registered in 2015 whose status has not been updated since, and two registered in 2026 that have not finished — and one uncontrolled supplement study. None has posted results. No medicines regulator has approved BPC-157 anywhere, and the reason two independent reviews give is that the clinical research needed to assess it has not been done.
compound.practitionerSummary:
Synthetic pentadecapeptide, sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, MW reported as 1419.556 g/mol, described as a partial sequence of body protection compound isolated from human gastric juice.

Mechanisms reported by the sources held here, all from laboratory work: angiomodulation — described as increasing angiogenesis where needed and decreasing it where not, including in tumour metastasis; nitric oxide stimulation; upregulation of VEGF, FGF and TGF-β; F-actin formation in fibroblasts; increased fibroblast migration and dispersal; increased phosphorylation of paxillin and FAK without change in the amounts produced; upregulation of anti-inflammatory transcription factors and downregulation of TNF-α; upregulation of growth hormone. Additional reported domains: neuroprotection with effects described on serotonergic, dopaminergic, opioid and GABAergic systems; cardioprotection including reported counteraction of neuroleptic-induced QTc prolongation; gastroprotection against ethanol, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, neuroleptics and capsaicin. Topical application reported to accelerate closure after alkali burn via granulation, re-epithelialisation and collagen deposition through ERK1/2.

**What the screen replaced.** This record previously said, under this heading, that no human evidence was held by this index, and noted that a PubMed search had returned 228 records none of which had been read. The screen recorded below read them. Three are human studies, so the earlier statement was true of the library and misleading about the world — which is exactly why it was bounded to the register at the time, and why the screen was the next thing to do.

Pharmacokinetics: one animal study held (BPC-014) — intravenous and intramuscular dosing in rats and beagle dogs; intact peptide half-life under 30 minutes; intramuscular absolute bioavailability about 14–19% in rats and 45–51% in dogs; degradation to peptide fragments and amino acids, excreted mainly in urine. No oral or subcutaneous data in any species, and nothing in humans.

Routes: subcutaneous and oral are both reported, and one source reports topical in an animal burn model. No source held here compares them, and none reports what fraction of an oral amount is absorbed intact — which for a pentadecapeptide is the question that determines whether an oral route means anything.

Safety, as reported: described as safe in recommended amounts by one source, with caution advised in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Rare reactions listed as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema, and rash. Paediatric safety not established. The angiogenesis caution and the reported anti-tumour effects sit in tension within the same source, and this index records both rather than resolving them.

Regulatory: no approval, no authorisation and no assessment in any jurisdiction, in anything held here.

Protocols: three sources, three different regimens, recorded separately and attributed. None cites a study establishing its amounts.

**Human evidence.** Three primary human studies identified by a PubMed screen on 13 September 2026, all uncontrolled: n = 2 intravenous safety pilot, n = 12 single-procedure injection for interstitial cystitis, n = 17 retrospective intra-articular chart review. No RCT exists.

**Citation crosswalk.** All twenty-two references the practitioner handbook gives for its BPC-157 entry are preclinical or reviews; twenty-one resolve to records in the screen (fourteen animal studies, seven reviews). The sole citation for tumour cell growth inhibition is a 2004 conference abstract in a human melanoma cell line, not indexed in PubMed. The cancer-cachexia claim traces to a 2018 review that states it is written before any clinical trial. A clinician following the handbook's citations will not reach human evidence, because there is none at the end of them.

**Primary preclinical studies read.** The orthopaedic systematic review (SRC-032; 35 preclinical and 1 clinical study included) is used as a map. Three primary studies it cites were read in full under CC BY: a rat myotendinous-junction defect model (BPC-012; Zagreb group), growth hormone receptor expression in cultured rat tendon fibroblasts (BPC-013; an independent group — receptor, not hormone), and rat and dog pharmacokinetics (BPC-014). The tendon, ligament, muscle and bone healing studies and the preclinical toxicology study it cites are not open access and are recorded as gaps.

**Registered trials.** ClinicalTrials.gov, 15 September 2026: NCT02637284 (phase 1, oral, healthy volunteers, placebo-controlled; registered 2015, status unknown), NCT07437547 (phase 2, acute hamstring strain, placebo-controlled; recruiting), NCT07803250 (pilot after rotator cuff repair, sham-controlled; not yet recruiting), NCT07752381 (single-arm supplement study; completed, registered after completion). No results posted for any. Recorded as registrations, not as evidence.
compound.unknownsSummary:
Whether BPC-157 does anything useful in people. Three human studies have been identified and none of them can answer that, because none had a comparison group — and the conditions they looked at are ones that come and go on their own.

Also unknown: how much, how often, for how long, by which route, what happens on stopping, what happens with prolonged use, whether the material sold under this name is what it says it is, and whether the effect on blood-vessel growth is a hazard in cancer or a therapeutic possibility — a question on which two research groups disagree in print and neither has human evidence.

One more thing is unknown in a different way. A 2006 review states that clinical trials in inflammatory bowel disease were carried out under three development codes. No report of them appears in this search, and a 2026 review states that no Phase II trial has been completed. This index cannot tell whether those trials were run and never published, or whether the characterisation is wrong. It is recorded as a lead.

Controlled studies in people have now been registered; none has reported. Until one does, the animal work — however much of it there is — remains the main body of evidence, and it cannot answer questions about people.

The volume of discussion around this compound is not evidence, and this record is arranged so that the two are not mistaken for each other.

claims.claimText: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide with the sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, described by the sources held here as a partial sequence derived from body protection compound found in human gastric juice.
claims.plainLanguageText: BPC-157 is a short chain of fifteen amino acids, made synthetically. Its sequence comes from part of a larger protein found in stomach fluid.
claims.interpretationNotes: Two sources agree on the derivation and one gives the sequence explicitly. This index records the derivation as the sources state it — the sequence is derived from a gastric protein — and does not extend that into a claim that the body produces this peptide, which the sources do not say and which is the inference most often drawn from it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Neither source held here cites an isolation or characterisation paper that this index has read. Whether the administered peptide is identical to any naturally occurring fragment is not established by anything held here.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives the fifteen-residue sequence, the molecular weight, and the category 'gastric pentadecapeptide', and lists Body Protection Compound-157 and Bepecin as other names.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a statement about the molecule.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: A PubMed screen conducted on 13 September 2026 returned 230 records and identified three primary human studies of BPC-157, involving 31 people in total. All three are small, uncontrolled, unblinded, single-site and published in the same journal. The remaining evidence identified by the screen is preclinical: 161 animal studies, one human-tissue preparation and three in vitro studies, alongside 48 reviews and 7 commentary pieces.
claims.plainLanguageText: Most of what is said about BPC-157 comes from laboratory and animal research. A search of the medical literature found three studies in people, together involving thirty-one participants. None of them had a comparison group, so none can show that an effect was caused by the compound rather than by anything else.
claims.interpretationNotes: This claim replaces one that said no human study was recorded in the sources held here. That was true of the library and said nothing about the literature, which is why the screen was run. The answer it returned is not the one the register implied: human studies exist. They are also not the kind of evidence that would support any of the uses attributed to this compound — a two-participant infusion pilot and two retrospective chart reviews of twelve and seventeen patients, none controlled, are hypothesis-generating at best. A systematic review published in 2025 searched three databases independently to June 2024 and included 36 studies, of which it classified one as clinical, and reported that it found no clinical safety data. Two independent screens reaching the same shape of answer is worth more than either alone.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about one database on one date under one set of criteria, and it is bounded to that. PubMed is not the whole of the scientific literature: it indexes neither conference abstracts nor most regulatory submissions, and a 2006 review asserts that clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease were conducted under the development codes PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736 — no report of which appears in this search. Those trials are recorded as a gap, not as evidence and not as absence. The interstitial cystitis study has been read in full. The intravenous study is verified at abstract level; an owner transcription of its body is held but unverified. The knee study is held at abstract level only. One record the screen's rule had classified as an animal study (Chang et al. 2014, PMID 25415472) was reclassified as in vitro on 15 September 2026, when its full text was read: it used tendon cells cultured from rats, not live animals.

evidence.interpretation: An IRB-approved study of intravenous infusion in two adults over three days, with blood work and vital signs before and after each infusion, reporting no measurable change in the biomarkers tested and no reported side effects.
evidence.populationModel: Two adults at a private clinic, both of whom had received intravenous BPC-157 before the study.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: A retrospective chart review of twelve women with moderate to severe interstitial cystitis, all of whom had previously tried pentosan polysulfate, each treated with injections into the bladder wall during a single cystoscopy at a urogynaecology practice. The outcome was a single five-point Global Response Assessment, collected when patients were contacted afterwards; the report gives both six weeks and, for most patients, four to six months. Cystoscopic change is illustrated for one patient only.
evidence.populationModel: Twelve women aged 39 to 76 at one urogynaecology practice where a co-author practises; participants paid for the material.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text held and read (Altern Ther Health Med 2024;30(10):12-17). It confirms the population, the single procedure and the self-rated outcome recorded from the abstract, and shows that the study was a retrospective chart review rather than a prospective one, with outcome timing reported inconsistently.

evidence.interpretation: A retrospective one-year chart review of seventeen patients given intra-articular BPC-157, alone or combined with thymosin beta-4, followed up by telephone survey with no validated instrument.
evidence.populationModel: Seventeen patients at one clinic; sixteen were reached for follow-up.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: An independent systematic review, two screeners, three databases, searched to June 2024: 544 records identified, 36 studies included — 35 preclinical and 1 clinical — and no clinical safety data found.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a review of the literature.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review characterising studies this index has not obtained. Its account of them has not been checked against the papers.

claims.claimText: The healing effects reported in laboratory studies include accelerated wound and tissue healing across tendon, ligament, bone, muscle, skin and gastric mucosa, with reported mechanisms including improved tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation.
claims.plainLanguageText: In laboratory work, the compound has been reported to speed healing across several tissue types, by encouraging the processes that rebuild tissue.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a description of what laboratory work has reported, with the tissue list kept as the source gives it rather than generalised to 'healing'. The specific mechanisms named — granulation, fibroblast recruitment, collagen formation — are what the source offers as the how, and are recorded because a mechanism makes a claim checkable in a way that an outcome alone does not.
claims.uncertaintyText: Preclinical, entirely. A result in an animal model is not a result in a person, and a mechanism operating in cell culture is not an effect in a body. The papers these practitioner sources cite have not been opened by this index, so the models, doses and routes behind this list are unknown here. Separately, three primary preclinical studies mapped by an independent systematic review have been read and are recorded as their own statements (BPC-012 to BPC-014); they cover a rat myotendinous-junction model, cultured tendon cells and pharmacokinetics, not the full tissue list above. The primary tendon, ligament, muscle and bone studies that could not be read are recorded as a gap.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists 'Helps heal tissues — promotes microscopic regeneration; improves tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation' among the effects reported in laboratory studies, with the tissue list given in its opening sentence.
evidence.populationModel: Laboratory studies, models not specified by the source.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists healing of wounds and injuries in muscles, tendons, ligaments, bone and skin, and increased blood flow to damaged areas, as effects consistently observed in animal studies and anecdotal report.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: The sources describe BPC-157 as angiomodulatory rather than simply pro-angiogenic: reported to increase blood vessel formation where needed and decrease it where not, including in tumour metastasis, and to stimulate nitric oxide production and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.
claims.plainLanguageText: The sources describe it as adjusting blood vessel growth in both directions rather than only increasing it — including reducing it in the context of tumours.
claims.interpretationNotes: This claim is recorded because of the tension inside it, not despite it. The same source that describes bidirectional angiomodulation and reports inhibition of tumour cell lines also advises caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Both are recorded, and the tension is recorded as a disagreement on this page rather than resolved by choosing the more reassuring of the two.
claims.uncertaintyText: 'Increased when needed, decreased when needed' is a strong claim and, as stated, an unfalsifiable one: it describes an outcome without a mechanism that would predict which direction occurs when. The source offers no criterion. Nothing held here establishes what determines the direction, or whether the bidirectional behaviour has been observed outside the specific models cited.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists BPC-157 as a 'potent angiomodulatory factor' that 'modulates angiogenesis — increased when needed, decreased when needed such as in tumor metastasis', and separately lists nitric oxide stimulation and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The source states that despite its ability to promote angiogenesis, BPC-157 is reported to inhibit and counteract increased VEGF expression and subsequent signalling, thus avoiding VEGF-tumorigenesis, and that it inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines and can counteract tumour cachexia.
evidence.populationModel: Tumour cell lines and laboratory models.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The same source advises using BPC-157 with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed — a caution that sits against its own account of bidirectional angiomodulation and anti-tumour effect.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: The practitioner sources held here report both subcutaneous and oral administration, and topical application in an animal burn model, without comparing them or reporting bioavailability for any route.
claims.plainLanguageText: Injection under the skin, swallowing, and application to the skin are all described. No source held here says how much reaches the body by any of these routes, or compares them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a claim because the oral route is the one a reader is most likely to act on and the one the sources support least. A fifteen-residue peptide taken orally faces gastric and intestinal proteolysis, and whether any survives intact is precisely the question the sources do not address. This index records that they report the route and records that they establish nothing about it.
claims.uncertaintyText: That an amount is reported for a route is not evidence that the route delivers the peptide. One animal pharmacokinetic study is now held (BPC-014): it tested intravenous and intramuscular injection in rats and dogs only. No bioavailability figure for oral or subcutaneous administration, in any species, appears in anything held here, and nothing held here addresses whether the peptide survives digestion.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives separate subcutaneous and oral amounts under 'Dosage', and lists an available injectable solution strength. It gives no bioavailability figure for either.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The source reports that topical treatment accelerated wound closure following an alkali burn, with a mechanism attributed to granulation, re-epithelialisation, dermal remodelling and collagen deposition through ERK1/2 signalling.
evidence.populationModel: Animal burn model; species not specified by the source.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: The sources held here report no approved product, no regulatory assessment and no approved indication for BPC-157 in any jurisdiction.
claims.plainLanguageText: There is no approved medicine containing BPC-157. No regulator, in anything this index holds, has assessed it for any use.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as an explicit claim rather than as an empty regulatory section, because an empty section reads as 'not yet filled in' and this is a finding. Two of the three sources are practitioner handbooks that name brand names and manufacturers for other compounds — including for tesamorelin in the same volume — and name none here.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about what the sources held here record. It is not a statement about the regulatory position in any particular jurisdiction, which would require a regulatory source, and this index holds none for this compound. Regulatory status also changes, and the most recent source here is from 2025.

evidence.interpretation: The source's 'Other Name(s)' field for BPC-157 lists only descriptive names and Bepecin, with no brand name, manufacturer or approval — in contrast with the same handbook's tesamorelin entry, which names Egrifta and Theratechnologies.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: Reported adverse effects are limited: one source describes BPC-157 as safe in recommended amounts, listing erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema and rash as rare reactions, and states that paediatric safety has not been established.
claims.plainLanguageText: The handbook describes it as safe at the amounts it recommends and lists a small number of uncommon reactions. It states that safety in children has not been established.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded with its provenance foremost. 'Reported safe in recommended dosages' is a statement by a practitioner handbook about amounts that the same handbook recommends, with no study cited for either the amounts or the safety. A short list of adverse effects is what one expects when there is no systematic collection of them, and absence of reported harm is not evidence of safety.
claims.uncertaintyText: No human safety study, no pharmacovigilance record and no systematic adverse-event collection appears in anything this index holds. A compound with no trials has no trial safety data, and a short adverse-effect list from a handbook is not the same thing. Nothing here addresses prolonged use, interactions, or use in any specific population.

evidence.interpretation: The source states that BPC-157 is reported safe in recommended dosages, advises caution in cancer and conditions where angiogenesis may need suppressing, and notes that redness and pain at the injection site may occur.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists rare adverse reactions as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia combined with hand oedema, and rash, and states that safety in paediatrics has not been established.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: None of the three identified human studies had a control group, a randomisation procedure or blinding; all three were conducted at private clinics and published in the same journal, and two of the three were retrospective chart reviews. In at least two, what was administered is not established by the report: in one the material came from a 503A compounding pharmacy the authors do not name, with no certificate of analysis or identity or purity testing reported, and another gave a second peptide to part of the cohort. The interstitial cystitis report states no ethics committee approval for the study it reports.
claims.plainLanguageText: The human studies that exist are small and have no comparison group. That means that if the people in them improved, the study cannot show whether the compound caused it. It is the kind of research that suggests what to test next, not the kind that settles anything.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a claim of its own rather than as a caveat on the one above, because it is the part that a reader will otherwise skip. 'There are human studies' and 'there is human evidence for this use' are different statements, and the distance between them is this claim. Uncontrolled studies of a condition that fluctuates — interstitial cystitis, knee pain — cannot separate a treatment effect from regression to the mean, from the procedure itself, or from expectation. The knee study gave some patients two peptides, so even its uncontrolled result cannot be attributed to this one.
claims.uncertaintyText: The interstitial cystitis study has now been read in full. It confirmed the absence of a control group and added that the study was retrospective, that no ethics approval is stated, and that the timing of the outcome is reported inconsistently. The intravenous study is verified at abstract level only, and the knee study is held at abstract level only.

evidence.interpretation: The full text states that the peptide came from a US 503A compounding pharmacy that does not wish to disclose its name, and reports no certificate of analysis, lot, identity or purity testing for it. It describes the study as a retrospective chart review of patients who had received an experimental treatment, and states no ethics committee approval for it.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text held and read (Altern Ther Health Med 2024;30(10):12-17). Each element read at printed pp. 13–14.

evidence.interpretation: The authors' stated limitations are sample size, ethnic variation and the lack of a sham control group, with biopsies not performed because of cost. They do not name the retrospective design, self-rated outcome or unnamed supplier as limitations.

claims.claimText: Every one of the twenty-two references the practitioner handbook cites for its BPC-157 entry is preclinical or a review. Twenty-one resolve to records in this screen: fourteen animal studies and seven reviews. The twenty-second, the only citation given for inhibition of tumour cell growth, is a 2004 conference abstract in a human melanoma cell line that is not indexed in PubMed.
claims.plainLanguageText: The handbook that clinics most often use for this compound lists twenty-two scientific references. None of them is a study in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: This is the crosswalk between what a practitioner source says and what it cites, and it is the most useful single fact this index holds about BPC-157. The handbook is not misrepresenting its sources: it says throughout that the findings are from laboratory studies, and it is accurate. What the crosswalk establishes is that a reader following its citations will not arrive at human evidence, because there is none at the end of them. Every mechanism in the entry — angiogenesis, nitric oxide, growth-factor signalling, neuroprotection, cardioprotection, gastroprotection — traces to work in rats, mice or cells.
claims.uncertaintyText: The crosswalk matched references by title against the screen rather than by identifier, because the handbook gives no PubMed identifiers and its bibliography is reproduced from an imperfect scan. Two references are near-duplicates of each other, which the matching preserved rather than merged. The melanoma abstract could not be located in PubMed at all, which is a statement about PubMed's coverage of conference proceedings as much as about the reference.

evidence.interpretation: The handbook's summary states that the healing effects are reported 'in laboratory studies' and carries superscript references 49 to 57 for them.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a statement about what the source cites.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

evidence.interpretation: The entry's statement that BPC-157 inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines carries a single reference, to a 2004 item in Melanoma Research at pages A14–A15 — an abstract supplement — reporting work in a human melanoma cell line.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A secondary source. Where it cites primary literature it does so by superscript, link or not at all, and none of those citations has been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: As of 2026, independent reviews report that BPC-157 has no approved formulation, no validated dosing regimen and no completed Phase II clinical trial, and that it is not approved by the FDA or other regulators for absence of sufficient clinical study.
claims.plainLanguageText: No medicines regulator has approved this compound, and the reason given is that the clinical research needed to assess it has not been done.
claims.interpretationNotes: The previous version of this record could say only that the sources held here reported no approval — an absence in a small library. Two independent 2025–2026 reviews, one of them searching patent databases and regulator websites as well as three literature databases, state the position directly. That is still secondary evidence: a review saying a regulator has not approved something is not the regulator saying it. But it is a considerable advance on silence, and it is checkable.
claims.uncertaintyText: No regulator's own record has been consulted for BPC-157. The approach that produced authoritative labelling for tesamorelin — querying the FDA's own interface — returns nothing for this compound, which is consistent with the reviews and is not the same as confirmation from the regulator. ClinicalTrials.gov was searched on 15 September 2026 (BPC-157, BPC 157, PL 14736, pentadecapeptide, body protection compound). It lists no completed controlled trial with results: a 2015 phase 1 registration with unknown status, a phase 2 registration recruiting since February 2026, a pilot not yet recruiting, and a single-arm supplement study, none with results posted. A registration is not a result and is not cited as evidence here.

evidence.interpretation: States that the compound has not been approved for use in standard medicine by the FDA or other global regulatory authorities, owing to the absence of sufficient and comprehensive clinical studies confirming health benefits in humans. Also notes that it was temporarily prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency in 2022 and, as at the review's writing, is not currently listed.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: States that the compound lacks FDA approval and that its use is banned in professional sport, while being increasingly used by clinicians and athletes.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review characterising studies this index has not obtained. Its account of them has not been checked against the papers.

claims.claimText: A systematic review written from an orthopaedic sports-medicine perspective (Vasireddi et al., HSS Journal, 2025), searching PubMed, Cochrane and Embase to 3 June 2024 with two reviewers, identified 544 records and included 36 studies: 35 preclinical and 1 clinical. It reports preclinical improvements in muscle, tendon, ligament and bone injury models, describes the included studies as level IV and level V evidence, and states that it found no clinical safety data.
claims.plainLanguageText: An independent review of the sports-medicine research on BPC-157 found 36 relevant studies. Thirty-five were animal or laboratory studies and one was a study in people, and the review found no safety data from studies in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a map of the literature, not as evidence about the compound. What the review says about the animal studies is its summary of them. The preclinical statements on this record (BPC-012 to BPC-014) cite the primary papers, which this index read, and never this review. The review's reference list was retrieved as PubMed metadata to identify which primary studies to seek; the ones that could not be read are recorded as a gap rather than cited through the review.
claims.uncertaintyText: Read at abstract level. The full text is in PubMed Central under an author copyright line with no open licence this index could confirm, so its per-study detail is not used. Its abstract summarises its one clinical study as seven of twelve patients reporting relief for more than six months after a knee injection. The abstract of the knee study held here (SRC-031) reports 17 patients, 16 reached, and 11 of the 12 given BPC-157 alone reporting significant improvement, without a breakdown by duration. The two are not necessarily in conflict, and the full texts that could settle it are not held. 'Level IV and level V' is the review's own grading.

evidence.interpretation: The abstract gives the databases, the search date, the two-reviewer screening, 544 records, 36 included studies (35 preclinical, 1 clinical), preclinical improvements in muscle, tendon, ligament and bony injury models, no clinical safety data found, and the grading of the included studies as level IV and level V.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a review of the literature.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The statement concerns what the review itself reports, so the review is the source, read at abstract level. Its characterisation of individual studies has not been checked against them, except for the three read in full (BPC-012 to BPC-014).

claims.claimText: In male rats with a surgically created quadriceps myotendinous-junction defect, which the authors report does not heal on its own, BPC-157 given by intraperitoneal injection or in drinking water was reported to abolish the leg contracture seen in every control animal, to improve walking and motor-function indices, to shrink the defect and prevent muscle atrophy, and to improve collagen organisation and vascularity at the junction over 42 days, with lower oxidative-stress and nitric-oxide levels, higher eNOS mRNA and lower COX-2 mRNA in the tissue than in controls.
claims.plainLanguageText: In one rat study, animals whose thigh tendon had been surgically separated from the muscle recovered movement and tissue structure when given BPC-157, while untreated animals did not. This is an animal result. It does not show what happens in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: Primary animal study, read in full. The outcomes are the authors' functional, biomechanical, macroscopic, microscopic and biochemical assessments against saline or water controls, recorded as reported. The study comes from the Zagreb group and rests its premise on that group's earlier muscle, tendon and ligament studies, so it extends that work rather than independently replicating it.
claims.uncertaintyText: One rat study, six animals per group and time point, in a lesion model created for it. Random assignment and blinded surgery and assessment are stated; the methods describe no sample-size calculation. Most comparisons are reported in figures, which this index has not re-analysed. The amounts used are rat amounts, not human ones, and are deliberately not reproduced here. A result in a rat myotendinous-junction model does not establish any effect in a human muscle or tendon injury.

evidence.interpretation: Twelve-week-old male Wistar rats, randomly assigned at six per group per interval; the quadriceps tendon dissected from the muscle under anaesthesia; BPC-157 at two dose levels intraperitoneally or in drinking water, against saline or water controls, with assessments at days 7, 14, 28 and 42. Surgery and assessment are stated to be blinded; the peptide is stated to be 99% pure by HPLC.
evidence.populationModel: Male Wistar rats with a surgically created quadriceps myotendinous-junction defect.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC8615275) on 15 September 2026 and read; sections 2.1–2.4.

evidence.interpretation: Leg contracture present in all controls and absent in all treated rats; improved motor-function and walking indices; smaller defect and preserved muscle fibre size against progressive atrophy in controls; earlier and better-oriented collagen type I; lower MDA and NO tissue levels, higher eNOS and lower COX-2 mRNA than controls.
evidence.populationModel: Male Wistar rats with a surgically created quadriceps myotendinous-junction defect.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC8615275) on 15 September 2026 and read; sections 3.1–3.3.

evidence.interpretation: The authors state that the study cannot provide precise information about the full mechanisms responsible, and frame the result through their group's earlier tendon, muscle and ligament studies. Funded by a University of Zagreb grant; no conflicts of interest declared.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC8615275) on 15 September 2026 and read; Discussion, Funding and Conflicts of Interest.

claims.claimText: In fibroblasts cultured from rat Achilles tendon, BPC-157 increased growth hormone receptor expression at both mRNA and protein level, rising with concentration and with time over three days. When growth hormone was added to cells pretreated with BPC-157, the number of viable cells, PCNA expression and JAK2 phosphorylation increased.
claims.plainLanguageText: In cells taken from rat tendon and grown in a dish, BPC-157 increased a receptor that responds to growth hormone. This is a laboratory finding about cells, not a finding about healing in a body.
claims.interpretationNotes: Primary in vitro study from a group independent of the Zagreb group, read in full, and recorded as a proposed mechanism, which is how its authors present it. The mechanism list on this record, taken from practitioner sources, includes 'upregulation of growth hormone'. This study reports increased expression of the growth hormone receptor in tendon cells, which is a different thing, and does not measure growth hormone itself. The authors also report that their own earlier study found no direct effect of BPC-157 alone on the proliferation of these cells.
claims.uncertaintyText: Cells in culture from rats; each experiment repeated three times with cells from a different rat, compared by t-test. The microarray result that prompted the study came from the group's earlier work. The authors state that culture cannot reproduce the environment of a healing tendon. The peptide was bought from a named supplier and no purity or identity testing is reported. No animal or human outcome was measured.

evidence.interpretation: Growth hormone receptor mRNA and protein rose with BPC-157 concentration at 24 hours and with time over one to three days, up to sevenfold at day three; with growth hormone added, viable-cell counts (MTT) and PCNA expression rose with BPC-157 pretreatment, and phosphorylated but not total JAK2 increased with longer pretreatment.
evidence.populationModel: Primary tendon fibroblasts from Achilles tendons of male Sprague-Dawley rats, passages 2 to 4.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC6271067) on 15 September 2026 and read; sections 2.1–2.3.

evidence.interpretation: The authors state that their earlier study found BPC-157 had no direct effect on the proliferation or PCNA expression of tendon fibroblasts, and that in vitro culture cannot mimic the environment of a healing tendon.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC6271067) on 15 September 2026 and read; section 3.

evidence.interpretation: Each experiment was repeated three times with fibroblasts from a different rat. The peptide was synthesised and purchased from a named supplier, with its sequence and molecular weight given and no purity or identity testing reported. Supported by the National Science Council of Taiwan and Chang Gung Memorial Hospital; no conflict of interest declared.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC6271067) on 15 September 2026 and read; sections 4.1–4.2, Acknowledgments and Conflicts of Interest.

claims.claimText: In rats and beagle dogs given BPC-157 intravenously or by intramuscular injection, intact peptide peaked in plasma within minutes, was eliminated with a half-life under 30 minutes, and could not be detected 4 hours after dosing. Absolute bioavailability after intramuscular injection was reported as about 14–19% in rats and 45–51% in dogs. In rats, radiolabelled peptide was broken down into smaller peptide fragments and amino acids, with urine the main route of excretion. Oral and subcutaneous administration were not studied.
claims.plainLanguageText: In rats and dogs, injected BPC-157 was broken down and cleared from the blood quickly. The study did not test it taken by mouth, and it was not done in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: The only pharmacokinetic study of BPC-157 this index holds, read in full. It is an animal study and says nothing directly about people. It matters to this record for two reasons: it replaces 'no pharmacokinetic data in anything held here' with a bounded animal result, and it leaves the oral-route question where it was, because oral administration was not part of it. The authors' description of their radiolabel results as proving metabolic safety is their interpretation and is not adopted here.
claims.uncertaintyText: Two species; in rats, six animals per time point, and in dogs, six animals across four dosing cycles; intravenous and intramuscular routes only; material the authors synthesised and purified themselves. The authors state that many methodological validations were omitted for space and that metabolites in tissues were not analysed. Measurements after the radiolabelled dose track total radioactivity, including breakdown products, not intact peptide. No figure here transfers to a person, to another route, or to material of other origin.

evidence.interpretation: After intravenous and single or repeated intramuscular dosing in rats, intact peptide peaked at 3 minutes, had an elimination half-life under 30 minutes, was undetectable at 4 hours, and showed intramuscular absolute bioavailability of 14.49% to 19.35% across three dose levels, with exposure rising linearly with dose.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC9794587) on 15 September 2026 and read; section 2.1 and Tables 1–3.

evidence.interpretation: In beagle dogs, intact peptide peaked within about 9 minutes of intramuscular dosing, had an elimination half-life under 30 minutes, was undetectable at 4 hours, and showed intramuscular absolute bioavailability of 45.27% to 50.56% across three dose levels.
evidence.populationModel: Beagle dogs, three male and three female.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC9794587) on 15 September 2026 and read; section 2.2 and Tables 4–6.

evidence.interpretation: After an intramuscular radiolabelled dose in rats, urine was the dominant excretion route; the parent peptide was the main plasma component at 3 minutes and was degraded into small peptide fragments within 10 minutes, with labelled proline predominating at 1 hour; radioactivity peaked in most tissues at 1 hour, highest in kidney.
evidence.populationModel: Sprague-Dawley rats, intact, bile-duct cannulated and jugular-vein cannulated.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC9794587) on 15 September 2026 and read; sections 2.3.1–2.3.4.

evidence.interpretation: The authors synthesised and purified the peptide in their own laboratory; state that metabolites were not analysed in tissues and that many methodological validations were omitted for space; and were funded by Chinese national and provincial science grants, declaring no commercial or financial conflict.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Open-access full text (CC BY) retrieved from Europe PMC (PMC9794587) on 15 September 2026 and read; Discussion, section 4.1, Funding and Conflict of interest.

claims.claimText: Tremblay states that BPC-157 is active orally but that more than half of an oral dose is lost to digestion, so an oral amount must be roughly double an injected one for an equivalent effect, and that injection is the more efficient route for any peptide.
claims.plainLanguageText: Tremblay says BPC-157 does work taken by mouth, but digestion destroys more than half of it, so an oral amount has to be about twice an injected one.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded because the index holds no comparable conversion rule from any source: the LaValle handbook gives regimens per route and never relates one route to another. This is a practitioner's working rule offered with a mechanism, not a measured bioavailability, and the amounts are on the protocol record rather than here. The speaker owns the company that manufactures and sells the compound, which is context rather than a verdict on the statement.
claims.uncertaintyText: No pharmacokinetic study supporting the ratio is held or cited. 'More than half' is his estimate rather than a measurement, and the conversion is not calibrated against any outcome.

evidence.interpretation: The conversion itself, the digestion reasoning, and the statement that injection is always the more efficient route.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

claims.claimText: Tremblay states that the repair peptides, naming BPC-157, TB-500 and thymosin beta-4, are dose related — the more taken, the more effect — and argues that they do not raise net cancer risk, because the additional cell divisions involved in faster healing are divisions that would have occurred anyway over a longer period.
claims.plainLanguageText: Tremblay says more of these repair peptides means more effect, and argues they do not raise cancer risk because healing faster uses the same number of cell divisions in less time.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded at critical importance because both halves are consequential and neither is supported by anything held. A dose-response assertion invites taking more; the cancer argument is reasoning from first principles, which is how he offers it, not a finding. It is reproduced because he makes it and because a reader meeting it elsewhere should be able to see what it rests on. The speaker owns the company that manufactures and sells these compounds.
claims.uncertaintyText: No dose-response study and no long-term human safety data for any of the three compounds is held. The cell-division argument assumes that healing is the only process affected and that total divisions are what matters, neither of which is established anywhere here.

evidence.interpretation: The dose-responsiveness statement and the cell-division argument in full, as he gives them.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

claims.claimText: Tremblay states that about 98 per cent of the BPC-157 studies indexed in PubMed were produced by one group of Croatian researchers.
claims.plainLanguageText: Tremblay says almost all the published BPC-157 research comes from a single research group in Croatia.
claims.interpretationNotes: A claim about the shape of the evidence base rather than about the compound, and useful for that reason: a literature concentrated in one group is a different thing from an equally large literature from many. The figure is his and is not verified here. The same turn continues into a second-hand allegation about that group's research conduct; that is hearsay about identifiable people and is deliberately not recorded anywhere in this index.
claims.uncertaintyText: The percentage is not verified. No bibliometric analysis of the BPC-157 literature is held, and no literature screen has been run for BPC-157 that would test it.

evidence.interpretation: The statement about the concentration of the PubMed literature in one research group.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

claims.claimText: Tremblay states, in 2019 and again in 2022, that injecting BPC-157 near an injury gives no advantage because the bloodstream takes the peptide up before it can diffuse through the intervening tissue, while injecting within the injured tissue does have a local effect and needs imaging to place accurately; in 2022 he describes hydrodissection, mixing BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 into the fluid used to separate a compressed nerve from the tissue pressing on it.
claims.plainLanguageText: Tremblay says injecting near an injury adds nothing, because the blood carries the peptide away before it reaches the tissue. Injecting into the injury itself does work, but needs ultrasound to place accurately.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded across both held transcripts because the position is the same in each, three years apart: near the injury is pointless, within it is not, imaging is needed. A derived summary of this collection characterised 2019 as calling local injection a myth and 2022 as a reversal. Reading both transcripts does not support that, so the position is recorded as consistent rather than as a change; what 2022 adds is a technique and a case, not a different view.
claims.uncertaintyText: No comparative pharmacokinetic study of local against systemic administration is held or cited. The hydrodissection account is a single unpublished case described second hand, and the procedure carries risks the source does not discuss.

evidence.interpretation: The 2019 statement: tissue in between, uptake by the bloodstream within a minute, a local effect only within the injury, and ultrasound to place it.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

evidence.interpretation: The 2022 statement of the same rule, together with the hydrodissection technique and the reported case.
evidence.populationModel: One patient, as described second hand by the speaker. Not a case report this index holds.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

claims.claimText: Tremblay states that injectors working without ultrasound guidance, who believed they had placed an injection correctly, were in the right place about 75 per cent of the time.
claims.plainLanguageText: Tremblay says that without ultrasound, people confident they had injected in the right place were right about three times in four.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded because it is the stated basis for the imaging requirement in the claim above. He attributes it to no named source, and the transcript is loose at this point, giving the figure once as a miss rate of a quarter; it is recorded as the accuracy figure he states and no further.
claims.uncertaintyText: No study is named and none is held. Whether the figure comes from a published comparison of landmark-guided against ultrasound-guided injection, or from impression, is not established.

evidence.interpretation: The exchange giving the accuracy figure for injectors working without ultrasound.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Read directly in the held transcript at the recorded turn.

notYetSupported.statement: That BPC-157 produces any effect in humans.
notYetSupported.why: Three human studies were identified by the screen of 13 September 2026, and none of them is capable of establishing an effect. All three are uncontrolled: two participants given intravenous infusions, twelve women treated in a single procedure and reviewed retrospectively from charts, with outcomes self-rated weeks to months afterwards, and a retrospective telephone survey of seventeen patients, some of whom received a second peptide as well. A study without a comparison group cannot separate what a treatment did from what would have happened anyway, and the conditions involved — interstitial cystitis, chronic knee pain — are exactly the kind that fluctuate.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A randomised controlled trial. Nothing smaller answers this question, and the existence of uncontrolled studies does not narrow the gap.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does BPC-157 produce any measurable effect in people, in a trial with a comparison group?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. The interstitial cystitis full text confirms it had no comparison group; nothing supplied could establish an effect.

notYetSupported.statement: What proportion of an orally administered amount reaches the circulation intact.
notYetSupported.why: Two sources report an oral amount and neither reports a bioavailability figure or a pharmacokinetic study. For a fifteen-residue peptide this is the question that determines whether an oral route delivers anything at all, and nothing held here addresses it.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A pharmacokinetic study comparing oral and parenteral administration, in any species, reporting plasma concentrations of intact peptide.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What proportion of an oral amount of BPC-157 reaches the circulation intact, and how does that compare with injection?

resolution.note: Checked 15 September 2026. The animal pharmacokinetic study now held (BPC-014) tested intravenous and intramuscular injection only. The 2015 registered phase 1 study (NCT02637284) lists oral pharmacokinetics as an outcome and has posted no results. Unchanged.

notYetSupported.statement: An effective amount, frequency or duration for any purpose.
notYetSupported.why: Three sources give three different regimens and none cites a study establishing any of them. This index does not average regimens and does not choose between sources, so it has no amount to state.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A dose-finding study, or any source that states the basis for the amounts it recommends.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Is there any amount of BPC-157 at which a measurable effect appears in people, and does the effect change with the amount given?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026 against the newly supplied human-study material; unchanged.

notYetSupported.statement: The safety profile of BPC-157 in humans, including with prolonged use.
notYetSupported.why: One identified study measured safety endpoints in humans: two people, three days, a panel of blood tests, no adverse effects reported. An independent systematic review searching three databases to June 2024 states that it found no clinical safety data at all. Nothing here addresses repeated use, long-term use, interactions, or use in anyone with a condition.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Human safety data from a trial or a registry.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What harms occur in people given BPC-157, including with repeated and prolonged use?

resolution.note: Checked 15 September 2026. Four registered studies list adverse events or safety monitoring; none has posted results. Preclinical toxicology is recorded as its own gap and would not settle this one.

notYetSupported.statement: Whether the compound's effect on blood-vessel growth is a hazard in cancer, a therapeutic possibility, or neither.
notYetSupported.why: Two research groups disagree about this in print, and the screen shows that neither side rests on human evidence. The concern is raised from mechanism in a 2025 literature and patent review; the counter-argument comes from the group that produced most of the preclinical work. The practitioner handbook's anti-tumour statement traces to a single 2004 conference abstract in a melanoma cell line, and its cancer-cachexia statement to a review that explicitly writes before any clinical trial.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: In vivo tumour model reports read in full, which would establish what was observed in what model at what exposure; and, for the clinical question anyone actually has, a study in people with cancer, which does not exist.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does BPC-157 promote or inhibit tumour growth in a comparable in vivo model, and at what exposure?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026 against the newly supplied human-study material; unchanged.

notYetSupported.statement: The regulatory position of BPC-157 in any named jurisdiction.
notYetSupported.why: Two independent 2025–2026 reviews state that no regulator has approved the compound and give the absence of sufficient clinical study as the reason. That is secondary evidence and this index records it as such: a review reporting a regulator's position is not the regulator. The FDA interface that supplied authoritative labelling for tesamorelin returns nothing for BPC-157, which is consistent with the reviews and is not confirmation from the regulator.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A statement from a named authority in a named jurisdiction, with a date.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What position has each named medicines regulator taken on BPC-157, and on what date?

notYetSupported.statement: What the laboratory studies behind every mechanism on this page actually did and found.
notYetSupported.why: Both practitioner sources cite their primary literature by superscript or by a link to the author's own website. None of those citations has been obtained or opened by this index.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The primary publications, obtained and read, with each mechanism checked against the paper reporting it.

resolution.note: Checked 15 September 2026. Three primary preclinical studies mapped by the orthopaedic systematic review were read in full under CC BY and are cited directly (BPC-012 to BPC-014). The papers the practitioner sources cite for each mechanism remain unopened, and the core tendon, ligament, muscle and bone healing studies are recorded as a separate gap.

notYetSupported.statement: The inflammatory bowel disease trials reported under the development codes PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736.
notYetSupported.why: A 2006 review states that the compound was "safe in clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease" under those codes, attributed to Pliva, Croatia. No report of any such trial appears in the 230 records the screen returned, and a 2026 review of the compound's development position states that no Phase II trial has been completed. The assertion is therefore either about trials that were never published, or a characterisation this index cannot check. It is recorded as a lead, not as evidence that trials happened and not as evidence that they did not.

notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Were the inflammatory bowel disease trials reported under PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736 conducted, and what did they find?

resolution.note: Checked 15 September 2026. ClinicalTrials.gov returns no study under PL 14736 or PL-14736. The only BPC-157 registration from before 2026 is an oral phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (NCT02637284), not an inflammatory bowel disease trial.

notYetSupported.statement: What the full texts of the three identified human studies report.

notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Access to the three full texts.

disagreements.topic: How much BPC-157, and how often: three sources describe three different subcutaneous regimens for overlapping purposes.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: Three books describe three different regimens for the same compound, and none of them says what that is based on. This index shows each one attributed to the book that reported it rather than combining them into a single figure.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The differences are not obviously explained by population, route or formulation, because none of the three sources specifies a population and two do not specify a formulation. What distinguishes them is the framing: one is a clinical handbook, one a consumer book citing its own website, one a set of worked personas. The most economical explanation is that no source is working from a dose-finding study, because this index holds no evidence that one exists.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A dose-finding study in any species, or any source that states the basis for the amount it recommends. Absent either, this index will continue to show three attributed regimens and no recommended amount.

positions.positionText: The Peptide Handbook gives 300-600 mcg subcutaneously daily for 30 days for general use, and 300-500 mcg twice daily where the use is injury-specific.
Optimize Your Health with Therapeutic Peptides gives a single recommended amount: 250 mcg injected subcutaneously twice a day.

The Complete Guide to Peptides uses 500 mcg daily in its joint and tissue repair example, and 250 mcg twice daily in its skin repair example — two different amounts within the same book, for different stated purposes.

disagreements.topic: Whether BPC-157's effect on blood-vessel growth is a reason for caution in cancer or a reason to investigate it against cancer. Two research groups disagree in print, and a practitioner handbook carries both positions in one entry.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: This compound affects the growth of blood vessels. Tumours need blood vessels to grow. Some researchers treat that as a reason for caution in anyone with cancer; the group that has done most of the research argues that the compound regulates vessel growth rather than simply increasing it, and reports anti-tumour effects. This is an open scientific disagreement, and this index does not settle it.
disagreements.explanationNotes:
The screen makes the shape of this disagreement clear. A 2025 literature and patent review raises tumorigenesis as a speculative concern arising from the compound's pro-angiogenic activity. The research group that has produced most of the preclinical corpus published a comment rejecting that reading, arguing that the compound is angiomodulatory rather than pro-angiogenic and reporting prominent anti-tumour potential in vivo and in vitro; the reviewed authors replied. The practitioner handbook carries both sides without noting that they are contested.

What the screen adds is the weight behind each. The pro-angiogenic finding is supported by an animal and cell study showing increased vessel density in a chick membrane assay, restored blood flow in a rat hind limb, and VEGFR2 upregulation in human endothelial cells. The handbook's anti-tumour statement carries one citation: a 2004 conference abstract reporting inhibition of cell growth in a human melanoma cell line, not indexed in PubMed. Its cancer-cachexia statement traces to a 2018 review that proposes the application and says in terms that it is writing before any clinical trial.

So the two sides are not symmetrical in evidence, and they are also not resolvable from what exists: a cell line is not a person in either direction, and neither position has human evidence behind it.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A study in humans with cancer, which nobody has done. Short of that, the in vivo tumour models themselves, read in full rather than through a conference abstract and a review — which would establish what was actually observed, in what model, by what route, and at what exposure.

positions.positionText: "Although BPC-157 is angiomodulatory, use with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed."

The same entry states that the compound avoids VEGF-tumorigenesis, inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines and can counteract tumour cachexia — citing, for the first of those, a single 2004 conference abstract in a melanoma cell line.
A 2025 literature and patent review raises the compound's pro-angiogenic activity as a possible route to tumorigenesis, as a concern arising from mechanism.

The principal research group's published comment rejects that reading, arguing the compound controls angiogenesis rather than simply promoting it, and asserting prominent anti-tumour potential in vivo and in vitro.

This index holds no regulatory document for this compound and cannot state the position in any named jurisdiction. The date is the date the sources were read.
